stem: A heart recipient calls the transplant clinic reporting new chest pain. According to urgent-contact education, how should the coordinator classify this symptom?

options.text: An urgent matter requiring prompt transplant team contact
A non-urgent matter appropriate for the next routine medication refill call
A symptom that never requires notification after transplant
A reason to stop all immunosuppression without medical guidance

explanation.rationale_correct: Chest pain is listed among urgent matters for which patients and caregivers should contact the transplant team promptly.

rationale_incorrect.B: Chest pain is categorized as urgent, not a routine non-urgent contact.
rationale_incorrect.C: Post-transplant education requires reporting chest pain to the team.
rationale_incorrect.D: Chest pain prompts team evaluation rather than independent immunosuppression cessation.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → §h. Communication → iii. Urgent matters

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → §h. Communication → iii. Urgent matters (chest pain); PDF p. 111 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Fourth 030700 item; distinct from rectal bleeding (cctc-3021) and FAST stroke (cctc-3017); anchor verified on Cupples p. 111.

stem: A liver transplant candidate on the waitlist asks why frequent clinic visits are still required while waiting. What education aligns with standard waitlist management references?

options.text: Patients must attend transplant clinic appointments on a schedule determined by disease severity or program protocol
Waitlisted patients are excused from all clinic visits until an organ offer
Only recipients after transplant need scheduled clinic follow-up
Clinic visits may be permanently replaced by annual phone calls only

explanation.rationale_correct: Waitlist management education includes attending transplant clinic appointments on a schedule determined by the severity of end-organ disease or program protocol while awaiting transplantation.

rationale_incorrect.B: Active waitlist management requires ongoing clinic attendance, not exemption until organ offer.
rationale_incorrect.C: Scheduled clinic follow-up applies during the waiting period as well as after transplant.
rationale_incorrect.D: References require in-person clinic scheduling based on disease severity, not phone-only follow-up.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → §b. Waitlist management → b.iii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Patients must attend transplant clinic appointments on a schedule determined by the severity of their end-organ disease or program protocol

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → §b. Waitlist management → b.iii. (required clinic appointments while waitlisted); PDF p. 102 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Fourth 030500 item; waitlist-phase coordination distinct from monthly post-transplant visits (cctc-3007) and community MD communication (cctc-3014); anchor verified on Cupples p. 102.

stem: During discharge medication teaching, a kidney recipient asks whether grapefruit is safe with their immunosuppression regimen. What counseling is MOST accurate?

options.text: Grapefruit may increase serum levels of certain immunosuppression medications and should be avoided unless the team approves
Grapefruit has no interactions with any transplant medications
Grapefruit should replace all oral immunosuppression doses
Grapefruit is required daily to maintain therapeutic drug levels

explanation.rationale_correct: Medication education includes food–drug interactions such as grapefruit, which can increase serum levels of certain immunosuppression medications.

rationale_incorrect.B: Grapefruit is specifically cited as interacting with immunosuppression drug levels.
rationale_incorrect.C: Grapefruit is a dietary interaction concern, not a substitute for prescribed immunosuppression.
rationale_incorrect.D: Grapefruit increases drug levels and requires caution, not mandatory daily consumption.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → medication management → drug–food interactions
primary_anchor.quote_hint: grapefruit, which increase serum levels of certain immunosuppression medications

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → medication management → Right way (grapefruit and immunosuppression interactions); PDF p. 108 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

stem: A heart transplant recipient starting mycophenolate mofetil (CellCept) asks which adverse effects are commonly associated with this medication. What teaching is MOST accurate?

options.text: Diarrhea, vomiting, leukopenia, neutropenia, and infections
Permanent cure of diabetes without monitoring
No gastrointestinal or hematologic side effects
Guaranteed protection against all post-transplant infections without risk

explanation.rationale_correct: Mycophenolate (CellCept) is associated with diarrhea, vomiting, leukopenia, neutropenia, and infections, requiring monitoring and patient education.

rationale_incorrect.B: Mycophenolate is immunosuppressive therapy, not a diabetes cure.
rationale_incorrect.C: Gastrointestinal and hematologic adverse effects are listed for mycophenolate.
rationale_incorrect.D: Immunosuppression increases infection risk rather than eliminating it.
